tagline: Grapes, places and vintages: how to order, taste and talk without sounding lost.
why: Wine is the default drink at business dinners, weddings and celebrations in Hong Kong, which became Asia's wine hub after scrapping wine duty in 2008. Wine talk can feel intimidating, but it rests on a few ideas: grape varieties, regions, vintages and how a wine tastes. Learn those and you can order confidently, compliment the host's bottle, and ask the questions that get wine lovers talking.

essentials.title: Grapes vs places
essentials.body: New World wines (Australia, US, Chile, NZ) are usually labelled by grape, like 'Cabernet Sauvignon'. Old World wines (France, Italy, Spain) are labelled by place, like 'Bordeaux', and you're expected to know which grapes grow there.

essentials.title: The big red grapes
essentials.body: Cabernet Sauvignon (bold, structured), Merlot (softer), Pinot Noir (light, elegant), Syrah/Shiraz (spicy), plus Italy's Nebbiolo and Sangiovese and Spain's Tempranillo.

essentials.title: The big white grapes
essentials.body: Chardonnay (from crisp to buttery), Sauvignon Blanc (zesty), Riesling (aromatic, can be sweet or dry), plus Pinot Grigio and Chenin Blanc.

essentials.title: France's key regions
essentials.body: Bordeaux (Cabernet and Merlot blends; the 'first growths'), Burgundy (Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; tiny prestigious plots), Champagne (sparkling), the Rhône (Syrah, Grenache) and the Loire.

essentials.title: How tasting works
essentials.body: Look, swirl, smell, sip. People describe body (light to full), acidity, tannin (the drying feel in reds), sweetness and finish (how long the taste lasts).

essentials.title: Vintage matters, sometimes
essentials.body: The vintage is the year the grapes were picked. Weather makes some years better, which matters most for top Bordeaux, Burgundy and Champagne.

essentials.title: Food pairing basics
essentials.body: Match weight with weight: big reds with steak, crisp whites with seafood, off-dry Riesling with spicy food, Champagne with almost anything fried or salty, including dim sum.

names.name: Bordeaux
names.what: France's most famous region, home of grand châteaux and long-lived reds.

names.name: Burgundy
names.what: France's Pinot Noir and Chardonnay heartland; its top wines are the world's priciest.

names.name: Champagne
names.what: The only sparkling wine that can be called Champagne, from northeast France.

names.name: Château Lafite Rothschild
names.what: First-growth Bordeaux that became a status symbol in China around 2010.

names.name: Domaine de la Romanée-Conti (DRC)
names.what: Burgundy's most legendary estate; bottles can cost tens of thousands of dollars.

names.name: Penfolds Grange
names.what: Australia's most famous wine, very popular in Asia.

names.name: Barolo
names.what: Italy's 'king of wines', from Nebbiolo in Piedmont.

names.name: Tuscany
names.what: Home of Chianti and the 'Super Tuscans' like Sassicaia.

names.name: Robert Parker
names.what: Critic whose 100-point scores shaped wine buying for decades.

names.name: Ningxia
names.what: China's leading wine region, winning international awards.

now.headline: Fine wine prices slumped
now.detail: After a 2022 peak, prices for top Bordeaux and Burgundy fell, and many collectors are selling.

now.headline: Young people drink less
now.detail: Gen Z drinks less alcohol, and wine sales are falling in many markets.

now.headline: Climate change
now.detail: Earlier harvests and heatwaves are changing classic regions; cooler places like England benefit.

now.headline: Lighter styles
now.detail: Chillable reds, lower alcohol and fresher styles are in fashion.

local.headline: Duty-free hub
local.detail: No wine tax since 2008 made Hong Kong a world centre for wine trading and auctions.

local.headline: BYO culture
local.detail: Many restaurants allow bringing your own wine, sometimes with free corkage on certain nights.

local.headline: Wine with Chinese food
local.detail: Bordeaux at banquets is a tradition, but Riesling and Champagne pair better with Cantonese dishes.

local.headline: Wine & Dine Festival
local.detail: The Hong Kong Wine & Dine Festival on the harbourfront each autumn is a big social event.

debates.question: Is expensive wine worth it?
debates.sides: Blind tastings often show people can't tell; enthusiasts say great wine is unmistakable.

debates.question: Natural wine: exciting or faulty?
debates.sides: Fans love its energy; critics find it funky and inconsistent.

debates.question: Screw caps or corks?
debates.sides: Screw caps prevent cork taint; corks are traditional and may help ageing.

debates.question: Old World or New World?
debates.sides: Elegance and tradition vs ripeness and value.
